title: The ceremony, plainly
hookLine: five Sikhs prepare amrit, share it, and teach the rehat
tomorrow: two days in, Jasleen oversleeps her prayers. did she just fail?

lines: A BENCH OUTSIDE A CLOSED DOOR.
cards: Sugar dissolving in water makes no sound at all. Steel stirring through it does: a low scrape, a soft ring against the bowl. Simran can't hear even that.
She's on a bench outside a closed door at the gurdwara, Jasleen's shoes lined up beside her, because the ceremony happens in a room of its own, away from the main hall. An hour later the door opens.
Jasleen comes out with damp hair and wet eyelashes, grinning, and says: it was sweet. Like, actually sweet.

teach.h: AN IRON BOWL, SUGAR, A KHANDA.
teach.b: Here's the ceremony, plainly, as the Sikh code of conduct sets it out. Five amritdhari Sikhs, the panj piare, the five beloved ones, prepare amrit in an iron bowl of clean water. Patase, small sugar puffs, go in.

One stirs it with a khanda, a double-edged sword, while the five recite set banis, starting with Japji. That's the sweetness Jasleen tasted: sugar in water, stirred with steel, while scripture is read over it.
Then each person comes forward, kneels, and cups their hands.

Amrit is given to drink, then sprinkled into the eyes, then onto the hair, and each time the giver calls out: Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki Fateh. The Khalsa belongs to God; the victory belongs to God.
The one receiving answers with the same words.
Then everyone drinks from the same bowl, whatever family they come from.
Then the five teach the rehat, the way of life, out loud. Now notice who does everything. The person taking amrit kneels and receives.
The five give. The five teach. That's the thing to tell a friend tonight: nobody takes amrit by themselves.
Someone always hands it to you.

how: The amrit ceremony is held in a separate room in the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib. Five amritdhari Sikhs prepare amrit in an iron bowl, give it to each person, and explain the rehat.

o: a priest blesses each person alone, in private

games.q: your friend wants to start running and says she'll do it solo: no club, no coach, no one. going by the ceremony, what's worth saying?
o: even amrit isn't self-served; let someone hand you the start.
solo is best; a real commitment shouldn't lean on anyone.
find one coach and let them do the work for you.
games.why: in the ceremony the person kneels and receives; the five prepare, give and teach. nobody takes amrit alone.

practice: Cup your hands in front of you, palms up, the way someone kneels to receive. Hold them there, light, not straining, for a few slow breaths. Then rest them in your lap and stay with the feeling of being handed something.

carryVoice: Your line: the five give. No one takes amrit alone, and no one has to. Talk soon.
